articles.title_orig: Xi and Putin begin highly anticipated meeting ahead of Trump's arrival in China
articles.title_zh: Xi and Putin begin highly anticipated meeting ahead of Trump's arrival in China
articles.content_orig:
China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin are meeting in Shenzhen , ahead of a summit of Asia Pacific leaders hosted by China
On Thursday the two leaders will attend an unprecedented trilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump on nuclear non-proliferation
Trump will fly to China later today from the Philippines, where he is attending another summit - images show him meeting India's Narendra Modi, Australia's Anthony Albanese and Japan's Sanae Takaichi
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr is among the Asean leaders offering Trump symbolic "wins", writes our North America correspondent
In Shenzhen, Xi's ambitions for China's tech-charged future will be on full display - and Beijing will be seeking a trade deal with Trump to avoid another tariff war
Edited by Gavin Butler with reporting from Jonathan Head in Manila, Laura Bicker, Steve Rosenberg and Stephen McDonell in Shenzhen and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
Laura Bicker Reporting from Shenzhen
There are a few key topics that will likely be up for discussion between Putin and Xi today.
Beijing maintains it is neutral in Russia's war in Ukraine - but has been accused of sending Russia military components and propping up the countryâs economy by buying oil and gas.
This is a delicate balance. Xi knows his relationship with Putin may damage Chinaâs connections in Europe, but doesnât want an end to the war that will destabilise a key ally and neighbour.
Putin and Xi will likely discuss energy supplies, and we'll be watching for any announcements on a proposed gas pipeline through Mongolia. Western sanctions have made Russia heavily dependent on China buying its oil and gas.
The two may also chat about their future relationship with the US and how to handle Trump in the trilateral meeting, as both have a shared goal to reduce America's global influence.
Xiâs main goal in these talks will be to keep Putin close, without allowing Russia's problems to become Chinaâs.
Laura Bicker Reporting from Shenzhen
President Xi is getting ready to host an unprecedented political
moment.
The Chinese leader will sit down with Russian leader Vladimir
Putin and US president Donald Trump for the first time on Thursday.
It is a chance for him to exude power and prestige as he greets
two leaders embroiled in wars they are struggling to end.
But first, he is having talks with Putin one on one.
The Russian-Chinese foreign policy partnership is working stably on the international stage, Vladimir Putin has told Xi Jinping at their meeting in Shenzhen, Russian state media report.
"Amid a challenging geopolitical environment, we are taking
a constructive approach to forming a fairer multi-polar world
order," Putin said.
Vladimir Putin's arrival in China for the Apec summit this morning made it to the front page of the People's Daily, the Chinese Communist Party's official newspaper, reflecting the importance China's leadership has attached to the Russian leader's visit.
The newspaper was also splashed with images of Xi Jinping meeting with six other world leaders attending the Apec summit.
The pictures all showed near identical poses of Xi shaking hands with leaders from Vietnam, Mexico, Peru, Chile, Canada and Papua New Guinea, with their respective national flags in the background. Those meetings took place on Tuesday.
Notably, this was the second visit to China this year for Vietnamese President To Lam, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Papua New Guinea's James Marape.
Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori and Chile's Jose Antonio Kast are making their first visits to China since assuming office.
Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are meeting now, according to Chinese state media.
An official schedule from Russia earlier indicated that Putin and Xi would hold bilateral talks at a business lunch.
Putin, who arrived in Shenzhen overnight, is also expected to tour Shenzhen University with Xi after lunch and attend a gala dinner tonight.
In some of his first comments to President Trump after they'd sat down inside the palace, President Marcos said he sent Jollibee fried chicken to Trump's party last night as a midnight snack.
Marcos claimed the Philippines' homegrown fast-food chain had "surpassed KFC in terms of popularity" in the US.
"Fantastic," Trump said in reply.
Jollibee is known for its fried chicken and sweet spaghetti with hot dog slices. The chain has over 100 stores in North America and caters to a massive Filipino diaspora, but it's also been winning local fans in recent years.
Ahead of their bilateral meeting, Marcos said the Philippines was looking to expand its decades-old relations with the US.
Philippine President Marcos says he gave Donald Trump a "condensed" tour of the MalacaÃ±ang presidential palace. Trump says what he saw was "fantastic".
Trump was seen climbing a grand hardwood staircase before signing a guestbook beside three Christmas trees. He then briefly toured the foyer with gold floor-to-ceiling trimmings and chandeliers.
Trump says the Philippines and the US have the same "architectural tastes".
"I love what you have done here," he says.
Trump says he is in Manila to "reaffirm one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific", adding that the two countries will expand defence cooperation.
"America stands with the Filipino people," Trump says. "Our alliance has never been better."
Osmond Chia Business reporter
The meeting with Trump and Xi will be a huge opportunity for Russian President Vladimir Putin to elevate the Kremlin's diplomatic standing.
Russia faces heavy sanctions imposed by Western and allied nations following its 2014 annexation of Crimea and its February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Putin is likely to make Ukraine a central focus of the talks, and will be keen for this summit to appear as a repeat of 1945's Yalta Conference, says Timothy Ash from the Chatham House's Russia and Eurasia programme.
That historic meeting brought together US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin to plan the final defeat of Nazi Germany and the post-war order.
Putin will hope "that Xi and Trump join him in deciding Ukraine's fate to the exclusion of Ukraine and Europe," Ash says.
Watch: Vladimir Putin lands in China's Shenzhen for Apec meeting
While Trump is in the Philippines, Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen in the early hours of Wednesday morning to attend the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit.
Putin will also be meeting with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
After a tour of the MalacaÃ±ang Palace lawn, Marcos leads Trump to a bamboo ensemble that plays what sounds like a folk song in Ilocano, his father Ferdinand Marcos Sr's language.
They then walk up a long staircase lined with Christmas ornaments (the Philippines celebrates the world's longest Christmas season).
Trump signs the presidential guestbook and views paintings at the palace foyer. He and Marcos are expected to hold a bilateral meeting soon.
The exact agenda of the meeting has not been released, but pressing issues between the two nations include the Iran war's impact on oil prices and China's manoeuvres in the South China Sea.
A 21-gun salute welcomes Donald Trump to the presidential MalacaÃ±ang Palace in Manila.
He then walks the red carpet at the palace lawn with President Marcos and inspects soldiers in line.
Trump tells the soldiers "good job", before greeting Marcos' secretaries of defence, finance and foreign affairs.
Donald Trump has arrived at the MalacaÃ±an Palace, where he's receiving a welcome ceremony.
A military band plays the US national anthem as Trump stands alongside Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent, reporting from Manila

articles.title_orig: Trump enjoys pomp and pageantry in Asia, administration tries to defuse fears on tech outages back home
articles.title_zh: Trump enjoys pomp and pageantry in Asia, administration tries to defuse fears on tech outages back home
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening , just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.
A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images North America hide caption
President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley , prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.
Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027 . Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.
Dressed in costumes for Halloween, students of Kids Campus SFCC play at the playground in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption
One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative .
Dressed in costumes for Halloween, students of Kids Campus SFCC play at the playground in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption
Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape .
Robert Pattinson attends the world premiere of The Odyssey in London in July. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Europe hide caption

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Analysts expect uncertainty around Nvidia 's future to linger despite another earnings beat, noting that much of the third quarter was already locked in before the turmoil that peaked in Jensen Huang 's resignation as CEO.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
Part of that increase reflects an extra week in the fiscal fourth quarter, which Melius Research estimated accounts for $9 billion to $10 billion of the sequential jump.
The company also lifted its fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%, even with China excluded from its data center compute revenue outlook.
"That's a team going full steam ahead, rather than just steadying the ship, and a clear signal that management believes next year can run just fine without Jensen Huang at the helm," said Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for Asia Pacific and the Middle East.
Still, even with the results that he called "nothing short of astonishing", Gilbert said "investors will still be left with the uncertainty of who and what comes next."
In his first statement since he resigned last week, Huang said before the results release that he was open to returning to the company. However, chair of Nvidia's board Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
The results should help ease some concerns created by Nvidia's recent leadership turmoil, said Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello, who described the figures as "solid" and broadly in line with the firm's expectations.
Colello expressed continued confidence that "the AI infrastructure buildout is real," pointing to Nvidia's shipments holding steady in the third quarter.
Michael Wilson, chief investment officer and chief U.S. equity strategist at Morgan Stanley, told CNBC TV that the results were "somewhat expected," with no major drop-off in Nvidia's business anticipated in the near term and guidance remaining "pretty constructive."
Wilson said AI remained a "desirable investment," with no slowdown in spending seen or expected from hyperscalers and some neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing. However, he added that investment may not continue at the pace investors expected six months ago.
Nvidia is widely seen as the bellwether for the broader AI industry and spending.
Gilbert shared that view, saying the AI trade can now "let out a small sigh of relief" after holding its breath for weeks. Nvidia had been "firing on all cylinders" before Huang's departure, he said, and its underlying fundamentals remained intact.
He pointed to Nvidia's supply commitments, which rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in three months, as well as its Vera Rubin platform, which has already brought in $20 billion.
"It's the clearest sign yet that the AI boom still has plenty of fuel in the tank," Gilbert said.
Nvidia shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading, though Gilbert said any rally is expected to meet resistance and "plenty of volatility" in the coming weeks, with the CEO search only just getting under way and investigations still playing out.
New U.S. export restrictions announced this week add another wrinkle. The Commerce Department will require licenses for shipments of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, citing the risk that they could be diverted to China.
Gilbert said the direct impact on Nvidia's forecasts appears limited because its guidance already assumed no China data center revenue, while China accounted for only around 2% of sales this quarter. However, new licensing requirements for shipments to places such as Singapore and Malaysia could slow some neocloud build-outs, he said.
Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes said fiscal 2028 is when sales to countries covered by the new restrictions would be expected to decline. He interpreted Nvidia's forecast as a sign that hyperscalers will take whatever supply becomes available elsewhere.
Nvidia said it is still studying the new Commerce Department rules but remains confident in its 75% growth target.
Colello pointed to longer-term risks around policy, international sales and hyperscalers developing their own chips, though he said Nvidia should remain an important player as the market expands.
He said investors will now be looking for the company to reaffirm its long-term outlook and show it can continue executing through the leadership transition.
"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," Colello added.
"Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump Meets Philippine Leader Before Flying to China
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump Meets Philippine Leader Before Flying to China
articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.
Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”
Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.
In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. The only event of substance on his schedule for the day — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump also met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
Palace history: Mr. Marcos hosted Mr. Trump at Malacañang Palace, where the Philippine leader spent much of his childhood. He left the palace in military fatigues 40 years ago when his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, was ousted. Read more ›
Lily Kuo contributed reporting.
At a lunch with Marcos, Trump said that the United States and the Philippines had just signed a trade deal, without giving more details.
“We didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both,” he said.
Xi has begun talks with Putin in Shenzhen, according to Chinese state media. The two leaders were expected to meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit ahead of a trilateral summit with Trump.
In his remarks to Marcos, Trump said the U.S.-Philippine relationship was “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific,” adding that the Philippines was a key pillar of security in the region.
“Our alliance has never been better,” Trump said.
Trump, while describing his administration’s support of arms sales to the Philippines, took a moment to praise the U.S. military’s efforts in Iran. “We’re doing very well in Iran, to put it mildly,” he said.
Seated next to Marcos at the meeting with Trump was the Philippine foreign affairs secretary, Maria Theresa Lazaro, the only high-ranking woman official in sight during days of high-level political meetings.
While Trump and Marcos met in Manila, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia was speaking to business leaders in Shenzhen, China, at the APEC CEO summit. Putin said his coming meeting with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping had “great potential benefits.”
Marcos said the two sides would not be signing an agreement on the Pax Silica artificial intelligence supply chain initiative today. The American-led initiative, an effort to build a China-free supply chain for the A.I. industry, has been met with resistance in the Philippines .
In his opening remarks, Trump hailed potential collaboration with the Philippines in the energy sector, noting that the United States is the world’s leading producer of oil and natural gas. He said that oil reserves in Venezuela, which he described as “our new acquisition,” and a new pipeline in Alaska would enable the United States to provide affordable, abundant energy supplies to its allies.
As their meeting began, Marcos said he had fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee delivered as a late-night snack for Trump on Tuesday.
“It’s providing extra energy for all the work that is in front of you,” Marcos said to Trump.
Malacañang Palace was once the home of an American president, William Howard Taft, who moved into the riverside property in 1901 as governor-general of the Philippines.
Trump signed a guest book at the palace, writing, “This is such a great honor. The U.S.A. loves you!”
The presidential palace is all decked out in Christmas décor. It may be early, but the Philippines starts preparing for the holiday as early as September.
Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, was in the lineup at the arrival ceremony, as was Dan Scavino, the White House deputy chief of staff. Howard Lutnick and Scott Bessent, two officials who have been feuding over the administration’s approach to exporting Nvidia technology, were also there, and stood next to each other. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, was also in the lineup.
President Trump was received on Wednesday by his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., at Malacañang Palace in Manila, where Mr. Marcos spent much of his childhood.
Forty years ago, he left the compound in military fatigues, when his family fled into exile after a popular uprising ousted his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.
Mr. Trump received a red-carpet welcome with full military honors at the palace, which sits by the Pasig River. The lavish compound was originally built as a summer house for a Spanish aristocrat

articles.title_orig: Interim Nvidia CEO Says It’s No Longer Sending AI Chips to China
articles.title_zh: Interim Nvidia CEO Says It’s No Longer Sending AI Chips to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The recent headlines about Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) have largely focused on who will replace Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week, and for good reason. But Wall Street is also starting to worry about something that could matter more to the stock: China.
Shares fell about 2% to roughly $160 on Monday morning, a day before Nvidia reports quarterly results. The stock has cratered 33% since early October. As investors gear up for the release, here's what the China-centric fears could mean for the tech giant.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Jensen Huang. Image source: Nvidia.
In a note published Sunday, analyst Dan Ives said scrutiny of Nvidia's China business and "possible loopholes in the region" could put about 10% to 15% of revenue "up in the air." He named Singapore as one of the loopholes.
That's different from losing direct sales to China. Nvidia already expects to sell no data center chips there this quarter, and its forecast reflects that. The new worry is sales to customers in other countries, like Singapore, whose chips may have ended up in China anyway. If regulators clamp down on those buyers, Nvidia could lose revenue it currently counts as coming from outside China.
Washington, meanwhile, is pushing hard. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on Nvidia to explain whether its most advanced chips reached China, and Huang has agreed to closed-door testimony before Congress.
UBS is already adjusting its guidance. On Monday, it cut its 2028 revenue and earnings estimates for Nvidia by 10%, citing potential export restrictions and data center delays, and lowered its price target to $240 from $300. It kept its Buy rating.
Nvidia guided for about $108 billion in revenue this quarter. If 10% to 15% of that disappeared, the company would lose roughly $11 billion to $16 billion a quarter, or about $43 billion to $65 billion a year at that pace.
That's a lot of money, but Nvidia would still be enormous without it. Even losing $16 billion, it would bring in about $92 billion this quarter, close to the $96.2 billion it reported in the second quarter, when revenue rose 106%.
As for the stock, Ives estimates Nvidia will earn $15.67 per share on an adjusted basis in fiscal 2028. At about $160, that's roughly 10 times earnings. If you cut his estimate by 15% to about $13.32, the stock would trade at about 12 times earnings.
Of course, that's a simplification (given that lost revenue doesn't translate perfectly into lost profit), but it shows how much bad news the price already reflects. Ives points out that peers trade at about 19 times next-year earnings.
UBS wasn't alone among firms that lowered their price targets but kept buy-equivalent ratings. Mizuho cut its price target to $220 from $250, saying the stock's roughly 33% drop from its October peak reflects a lost Jensen Huang premium. It called Nvidia "set up attractively with a strong roadmap." TD Cowen cut to $200 from $275. With a "still-strong demand backdrop, it's hard to see Street numbers coming down materially in the near term," the firm said, but it warned the uncertainty could leave the AI infrastructure trade "in limbo."
Ives kept his $225 target and Outperform rating.
The biggest risk could be what investors don't know yet. Nvidia has been hit by export policy before: Ives notes that charges tied to its H20 chip last fiscal year showed "how rapidly policy can strand inventory."
On Tuesday's call, listen for whether the $108 billion forecast held, how much revenue management ties to Singapore and other parts of Asia (if mentioned), and whether next quarter's guidance sets aside more.
If the hit lands near 15%, the math suggests Nvidia still isn't expensive. For long-term investors interested in semiconductor stocks , that makes this a stock worth buying in stages, keeping some cash available in case Tuesday brings more bad news.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.
While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.
Jonathan Ponciano has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

articles.title_orig: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.title_zh: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_orig: Trump wants to show strength in China, but a series of technological snafus raises concerns at home
articles.title_zh: Trump wants to show strength in China, but a series of technological snafus raises concerns at home
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump does not view a potential sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China as a concession — but stressed no meeting has been confirmed.
• Trump in Asia: Donald Trump is speaking at a state banquet alongside Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Manila. Later, he flies to China’s high-tech hub Shenzhen, where leader Xi Jinping is hosting a summit that will showcase a vision of the nation’s unrelenting rise .
• Historic trilateral: Trump’s trip includes an unprecedented joint meeting with the leaders of China and Russia . He may also meet with Kim Jong Un , should the North Korean leader travel to China. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump does not view a potential sit-down as a concession — but stressed no meeting has been confirmed.
• Xi slams “protectionism”: At the APEC summit, Xi pitched China as a defender of the globalized economy . While he did not mention the US, his speech appeared as Beijing’s counterpoint to the US effort to limit China’s access to high-end technologies — and keep Chinese high-tech out of certain global supply chains.
President Donald Trump touted a potential nuclear energy deal with the Philippines as he sat down with his counterpart Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for a bilateral meeting in Manilla.
Washington has expanded its defense cooperation with Manila, a mutual defense treaty ally, with the Trump administration approving $5 billion in approved arms sale.
One of the Philippines’ key defense challenges is China’s push to solidify claims over disputed territories in the South China Sea, where vessels from the two nations often clash.
Trump said he was not worried about the tension. “I’m not concerned about that at all. That’ll be taken care of,” he said. The expansive waterway is one of the most contested regions of the world.
Trump said the alliance between Washington and Manila “has never been better.”
“I very much appreciate your welcoming me and us back to the Philippines as we reaffirm one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific,” Trump said told Marcos Jr.
Trump received a red-carpet welcome with full military honors as  Marcos Jr. greeted him at the Malacañang Palace in Manila.
President Marcos spent much of his childhood at the palace as his father ruled the country under a tight dictatorship before his family fled into exile forty years ago.
Malacañang became the residence of the American Governor-General William Howard Taft in 1901, during the period of American rule following the Spanish-American War.
The leaders of Russia and China touted the stability of their relationship and its benefit to the world order during a bilateral meeting Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
President Vladimir Putin said Russia-China relations are “on the rise” and that both countries are taking a constructive approach to shaping a fairer, multipolar world order, Russian state media TASS reported. Putin also said the foreign policy coordination between the two countries remains stable.
China’s leader Xi Jinping said the relationship between Beijing and Moscow serves as a model for a new type of relationship between great powers, TASS reported.
On Thursday, both leaders are set to sit down with US President Donald Trump for unprecedented trilateral talks . Putin earlier said he expects “considerable potential benefits” from the discussions.
As world leaders descend on the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit this week, life for the tech hub’s 20 million residents will be far from ordinary.
All roads near the conference venue in the city center are subject to strict traffic controls. And no non-local vehicles are allowed to drive in the city’s six main urban districts.
Drivers are also being encouraged to switch to public transport. Those who do not drive for four consecutive days are eligible for a 100-yuan ($15) public transport subsidy. As of Monday, nearly 2 million vehicle owners had applied for the scheme. Fares for subways and buses are also cut by half during APEC.
Companies have also been encouraged to let their employees work from home to ease commuting pressures. And all primary and junior high schools will be shut from November 17-20 for a fall break.
The skies will be quieter too — the city has banned drones, kites, balloons and other flying objects from November 11 to 21.
While the roads may be relatively empty, they’ve been beautified with blooms, most of them bougainvillea — Shenzhen’s official flower. Flowers have been installed on over 600 bridges across the city, stretching for a combined length for over 360 kilometers (224 miles), according to a local state-owned outlet .
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday he expects “considerable potential benefits” from his trilateral meeting with China’s leader Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump, Russian state media TASS reported.
Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Putin highlighted a “tectonic shift” in the global economy, with the Asia-Pacific region at its center, TASS reported.
Putin said the European Union has failed to adapt to the loss of Russian energy, and that Brussels is losing its position, according to TASS. He also touted his country’s economic growth and said Asia-Pacific currently accounts for 53% of Russia’s foreign trade.
Putin said he expects support for Russia’s bid to chair APEC and host its summit in 2035, TASS reported.
The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting Thursday — the first ever between the leaders of the three countries — is expected to focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic the US president said could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states. Trump has also said he plans to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping hinted that China’s technology is on par with Silicon Valley’s by touting its own Greater Bay Area at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
“Asia-Pacific is home to the world’s most important Bay Area economies, which are characterized by distinct features such as openness, synergy, and spillover effects,” Xi told business executives at the APEC summit, which President Donald Trump will attend.
Without mentioning the San Francisco Bay Area, home to Silicon Valley, Xi touted China’s own tech capital.
The Greater Bay Area is Beijing’s strategic initiative linking Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Macau, and several other Chinese coastal cities into an integrated economic and high-tech powerhouse.
Shenzhen has launched tech advances that have put Trump and Xi on a collision course over access to raw materials, advanced chips, and lucrative markets.
In the tech hub, Xi said, robots work in factories, robot dogs work on farms and drones deliver food.
China supplies the vast majority of the world’s humanoid robots , but has been cut off from its largest export market as the US government moves to curb its reliance on foreign technology.
At a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders in the Philippines, President Donald Trump fondly recollected his ties with the country’s former dictator, who fled to Hawaii in 1986 following a popular uprising against his rule.
“I just don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” Trump told Philippines leader Bongbong Marcos, son of former dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr, who ruled the country under martial law.
The Marcos family plundered the country’s coffers before they fled to exile in Hawaii in 1986 carrying crates of gold, cash and jewels.
Trump and Marcos family are old acquaintances. Marcos Sr.’s wife, Imelda, now 97, and Trump attended parties together in New York and were photographed side by side in 1991.
“Great family, great family legacy and highly respected in his country,” Trump told Marcos Jr. the last time they met face to face in July 2025 in Washington.

articles.title_orig: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
articles.title_zh: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
articles.content_orig:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea , stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam , which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017 , after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title_orig: NC approves Duke Energy rate hikes, new rules for data centers
articles.title_zh: NC approves Duke Energy rate hikes, new rules for data centers
articles.content_orig:
Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand.
After opening in downtown Raleigh one year ago, Alejandro Leon Jr., owner of Olé Sports Bar and Lounge, said a new challenge is on the horizon for his establishment: Higher electricity bills.
“We’ve been eating that up and now unfortunately with
that spike its obvious that the consumers are going to have to pay all that up
front. Very unfortunate," Leon said.
Leon says the rate hike would put business owners like himself in a crunch.
“I was pretty disappointed that North Carolina approved the
spike," Leon said.
For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job.
Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up.
“I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said.
About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect.
The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests.
Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills.
The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season.
According to projections released Tuesday by Duke Energy, a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month would see the following increases:
Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina):
Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region):
That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges.
Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans.
Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills.
The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled.
Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs.
Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth.
“We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.”
For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect.
Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding.
“I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said.
The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days.
For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts.
The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas.
Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission.
Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure.
Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. Without additional safeguards, other customers could be left paying for infrastructure if anticipated data center demand fails to materialize or companies leave prematurely.
New financial requirements for qualifying data center projects and expansions include:
The commission also established requirements for data centers to temporarily reduce electricity demand under certain circumstances to help maintain grid reliability.
Duke said Tuesday that regulators retained many of the company's existing data center requirements while adding financial protections intended to shield other customers from the costs and risks of serving new facilities.
Environmental advocates welcomed the new financial requirements while calling for additional measures to address the costs of generating electricity for data centers.
“This is a big step forward to ensuring that data centers pay their fair share of the costs of connecting to the grid,” said Will Scott, North Carolina policy director for the Environmental Defense Fund. “Now we need to take the next step and enable them to pay for their own new clean energy and batteries to avoid regular customers bearing the cost of unnecessary new gas plants.”
Duke indicated in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday that it is evaluating the data center provisions and will continue working with customers and other stakeholders on implementation.
Monday's rate decisions came alongside a separate ruling approving Duke's latest long-term energy plan, which extends the operation of some coal plants and calls for nearly 3,850 megawatts of new natural gas generation, alongside additional solar generation and battery storage.
The decisions come ahead of the planned merger of Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress into a single utility on Jan. 1, 2027.
Duke must now work with the Public Staff, the state agency representing utility customers, to finalize its revenue calculations before the new rates take effect.
For Brooks, the immediate concern is how to stretch her household budget even further. She is considering taking another part-time job, even if it means sacrificing time with her grandchildren.
“It's just that it's so high that you're struggling to pay because you need to keep your lights on,” Brooks said. “You gotta have your refrigerator so you can put your stuff in it. It's just heartbreaking.”

articles.title_orig: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
articles.title_zh: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
articles.content_orig:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.
California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.
Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.
California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".
In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.
The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.
In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.
In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning.

articles.title_orig: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.title_zh: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.content_orig:
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

articles.title_orig: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.title_zh: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title_orig: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.title_zh: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”
