articles.title_orig: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
articles.title_zh: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
articles.content_orig:
Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO.
Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week.
"We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that."
While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital.
Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company.
Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion.
More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report.
Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call.
"The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said.
Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases.
It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang.
Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal.
A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter.
But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups.
"There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward,"
Plenty of big questions remain.
Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China.
China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China.
Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips.
None of that is stunting growth.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this."

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.content_orig:
Video captures the moment prayer beads hit Pope Leo near his eye as he rode through Lima in the popemobile. (Credit: Reuters)
Pope Leo XIV broke his silence Monday after being struck in the face by a rosary thrown by a worshipper in Peru, joking about the incident while also revealing details for the very first time about his cancer diagnosis and major surgery which took place before his recent trip to South America.
The pope, who had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13, after doctors found a cancerous tumor , told reporters on the flight home to Rome that he has not fully recovered, but said he was determined to complete the long-planned 12-day journey.
"Just over a month ago, as everybody knows, I underwent rather major surgery," Leo, 71, said during a roughly 45-minute news conference on board the papal plane returning from Lima, Peru.
POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY
Pope Leo XIV, flanked by Director of the Holy See Press Office Matteo Bruni, meets with journalists on the return flight from Latin America, Monday, in Lima, Peru. (Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
"But from the very beginning, I had in mind that this trip had been planned and that I was going to make it happen."
The pontiff credited his recovery to prayer, medical care and personal determination.
"So, with God's help — and I firmly believe in the power of prayer, as I have literally received messages from all over the world — together with a certain personal determination, which I also have, and with the help of the doctors, it proved to be possible."
Despite the demanding itinerary that included multiple flights and appearances before massive crowds in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, Leo acknowledged that he is still regaining his strength.
POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE
Pope Leo's 12-day tour began in Uruguay and went through Argentina before ending in Peru. (Andrew Medichini/AP Photo)
"I must say that I am not at 100%, but I am doing quite well. Stamina is a gift I have received from the Lord," he said.
The pope also revealed that his cancer diagnosis came as a shock after doctors found an abnormality during a routine annual medical examination.
"The initial news came as a surprise. There were no symptoms — I felt fine," he said.
"It was discovered during some medical tests, as part of what you might call a check-up: a routine annual examination that I have been having for many years."
Leo said the abnormality initially appeared as a shadow on his lung before additional testing revealed a tumor.
POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS
Pope Leo XIV addresses the media aboard the flight from Lima to Rome. (Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
"A biopsy then confirmed that it was a tumor," he said, before adding that he had decided to get it done "right away."
"By the grace of God, I remained calm," he added.
The surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer . The pope was discharged four days later.
"No further treatment is necessary. However, as a precaution, I will need to continue having these routine check-ups, simply to keep an eye on things, as is normal," he explained.
The Vatican cleared the pontiff to move forward with his South American trip after medical evaluations in late October.
The journey, which began Nov. 6, marked Leo's first papal visit to Latin America. He also holds Peruvian citizenship and spent roughly two decades serving as a missionary and bishop in Peru before taking on leadership roles at the Vatican.
POPE LEO XIV HIT IN THE FACE BY FLYING ROSARY DURING FAREWELL MASS IN PERU, VIDEO SHOWS
Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a farewell Mass in Lima, Peru. (Pilar Olivares/Reuters)
It was while riding in the popemobile through huge crowds toward the Mass in Lima on Nov. 16 that Leo was struck near the eye by a rosary thrown from the crowd.
"The affection shown by the Peruvian people, including the person who, with such great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary, is something one carries in one's heart — or perhaps in one's eye," he joked about the incident.
"These are experiences that leave a lasting mark on one's life."

"They bear witness to genuine enthusiasm, deep faith, and the desire to receive the Lord's blessing," he added before describing the crowds' devotion.
"Some even tried to get past the National Police barricades. They simply wanted to live, feel, and experience this faith," he said.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.title_zh: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, a ministry spokesperson said in response to a media query.
ALSO READ: China expands export control on precursor chemicals to US, Mexico, Canada
Guided by the important consensus reached between the leaders of the two countries, China and Canada have held multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations in the spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation, reaching a supplementary joint arrangement on trade issues of mutual concern, the spokesperson said.
The two sides also reached positive consensus on economic and trade issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment, according to the spokesperson.
READ MORE: Commerce ministry: China willing to lengthen cooperation list with Canada
The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Both sides will expedite their respective domestic procedures to put the agreed measures into effect as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.
READ MORE: China and Canada agree to address EV, rapeseed issues
The spokesperson added that the two countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations.
The preliminary joint arrangement between China and Canada was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

articles.title_zh: Nvidia rejects Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO despite pressure from Silicon Valley
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia’s board has made clear that it will not bring Jensen Huang back as CEO after shareholders and his fellow tech bros called for him to be reinstated .
Huang resigned as head of the AI chipmaking company after he admitted to an affair with a Chinese executive suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
“Jensen Huang, voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia’s board, said during an earnings call Tuesday. Executives refused to take questions from investors about the scandal.
Nvidia’s better-than-expected third-quarter earnings report caused its stock to pop in after-hours trading. Nvidia’s stock sat at $155.46 at the closing bell, and just thirty minutes later, it spiked by about 4 percent to $161.69.
The company reported revenues of $115.8 billion, beating Wall Street’s estimates of around $109 billion.
On November 8, the day Huang admitted the affair to employees, Nvidia said it would be conducting an investigation following reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang stepped down last Thursday and was replaced by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, while the company looks for a permanent CEO.
Over the weekend, an online petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia’s CEO garnered more than 100,000 signatures , including around 60,000 from shareholders, 6,000 from current Nvidia employees and 1,000 from former employees, according to reports.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney publicly backed the effort, and there was a report that Huang had discussions with allies about possibly returning to the helm .
One ally told the Financial Times that they were convening a “war room” of tech executives to reinstate Huang and would try to get support from the White House.
President Donald Trump , who has close ties to Huang and called him a “very high quality person” after the scandal broke, insisted he had no idea that U.S. intelligence found Huang’s mistress, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. But the New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to take action.
Earlier Tuesday, Huang released his first public statement since leaving Nvidia, admitting that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote on X.
Huang acknowledged the push from supporters to reinstate him as Nvidia’s CEO and said he’d be “honored to answer these calls.”
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.
“NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
But, as Nvidia’s board said during the earnings call later Tuesday, that won’t be in the cards — for now.

It declined 6% on Nov. 6 to close at 57,434.77, down more than 20% from a record 72,366.34 hit on June 25. A 20% fall is considered to be a technical bear market, though analysts and academics warn that a decline alone does not make a true bear market.
A landslide victory in U.S. midterm elections by the Democratic Party earlier this month rattled investors, stoking fears of a slowdown in data center construction given that many candidates pledged stricter regulations for these projects.

articles.title_orig: Do not eat these breakfast items, says USDA health alert
articles.title_zh: Do not eat these breakfast items, says USDA health alert
articles.content_orig:
Published on Nov. 17, 2026
The issue was discovered when a firm notified FSIS that they had received FDA-regulated item that had been recalled
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is warning consumers not to eat certain ready-to-eat meat products after discovering they may contain an ingredient contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes.
The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) issued a public health alert on Saturday, Nov. 14, for products containing FDA-regulated biscuits recalled by C.H. Guenther & Son. The issue was discovered after a company notified FSIS that it had received the recalled biscuits. The notice states that the agency may identify additional products as the ingredient recall progresses.
The good news is that no one has reported a confirmed illness linked to the products.
Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
The affected product is the 9.5-ounce Mmm! Meals Made in Minutes Biscuit & Sausage Gravy. Consumers should check for lot codes or “Use By” dates ranging from Nov. 12 through Nov. 18, 2026, and establishment number EST. 51248. The products were distributed in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Texas. The agency also provided product labels online .
As with most recalls , anyone who purchased the affected products should not eat them. FSIS advises consumers to throw them away or return them to the place of purchase, as is common with recalls . Retailers should also not sell or serve the products.
Listeria can cause listeriosis, a serious infection that, according to the USDA, primarily affects older adults, pregnant women, newborns and people with weakened immune systems. Symptoms can include fever, muscle aches, headache, stiff neck, confusion and loss of balance. In pregnant women, infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery or a life-threatening infection in newborns.
People in higher-risk groups who develop flu-like symptoms within two months of eating potentially contaminated food should seek medical care and tell their health care provider about the exposure, the USDA states.
Consumers with questions can contact the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 888-674-6854 or email [email protected] .

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump has arrived for his high-stakes trip to Asia, and took a range of questions on subjects from Iran to Deutsche Bank leaking details about his tax.
The president landed in Manila, Philippines, for the initial leg of his trip on Tuesday and answered rapid-fire questions from the press while meeting with other leaders.
Asked about a possible Iranian threat to Washington, D.C., he said that, if there were an attack, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
The question was about CNN reporting that U.S. intelligence suggested the country was planning to target senior members of Trump's administration with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the U.S. capital.
"We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," Trump said. CNBC has not independently verified CNN's report.
But the president also said he believed his administration was "very close to getting it done" when it came to the Iran war.
While Trump was airborne, the Financial Times reported Deutsche Bank had mistakenly leaked details of his taxes in March 2017, during his first presidential term. The mistake was kept from the White House at the time, according to the FT.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years. "Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
Asked about the situation in Manila, the president said, "I paid a lot of tax."
"They shouldn't have done it. It's illegal for them to do it," he added.
Trump was also asked about Nvidia 's announcement on Tuesday of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company, which reports earnings later on Tuesday, is reeling from the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned last week after having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy.
"It's a great company. It's a great idea," Trump said.
Trump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
He is also due to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Xi. Asked by a reporter if he would have a separate meeting with only Putin, Trump said: "I don't know, but I would, if it's available, I would do that. He's coming. I mean, it's really with the guests. I am the guest of President Xi."
Trump met the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping in the Philippines and the prime minister of Thailand. He is due to China on Wednesday.
Speaking at a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders as the event wrapped up for the day, Trump touted his record during his second term, citing investment into the U.S., trade deals made with countries represented by attendees at the dinner, energy infrastructure buildouts and America's AI industry.
Trump, who has led a campaign to rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence," or "SI," told leaders around the table that the U.S. is "leading the world" in the technology.
"We have the world's most powerful SI ecosystem," he said. "We're leading everybody by a lot, and we hope to keep it that way, and we will keep it that way."
He added that the U.S. has "the strongest and most capable military on the planet," pointing to investments in the armed forces and the country's defense sector.
"We make the greatest equipment. You saw that in Venezuela. You see it in Iran. You see it everywhere," Trump said.

articles.title_orig: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.title_zh: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.
The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.
Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.
The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.
“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.
As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.
Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.
As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.
In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.
Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.
Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.
“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”
The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.
Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.
“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.
Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.
Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.
The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.
China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.
Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.
Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.
The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.
In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.
The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.
“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.
For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.
Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.
“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.
Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.
US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.
By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent , while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.
Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.
A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.
“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”
US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.

articles.title_orig: Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
articles.title_zh: Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Leaders of the U.S., China, Russia and other major Asia-Pacific economies face a series of critical issues from wars to tech security as they gather for an annual summit this week.
Since the last APEC leaders' meeting, China's tensions with Japan have escalated . Barely stabilized U.S.-China relations face new tests in the wake of Washington's scrutiny of Nvidia 's China chip sales. And the Iran war , now in its ninth month, is still pressuring global energy prices, while the Russia-Ukraine war has dragged on.
But expectations are low for any breakthroughs.
Meanwhile for Beijing, host to this year's series of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings, the multilateral gathering is yet another venue to build its global influence. Chinese President Xi Jinping met Tuesday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the President of Vietnam To Lam . Vietnam is hosting next year's APEC meetings.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen early Wednesday morning, where he was greeted by Chinese Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi, according to Chinese state media. U.S. President Donald Trump is in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit before heading to Shenzhen.
Here's what's at stake this week:
Trump and Xi are expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting Wednesday and Thursday. Their summit around the gathering last year in South Korea ushered in a one-year trade truce of lower tariffs and some rare earths flows, which was extended by two months, to January 2027.
In this week's summit, Trump does not plan to raise the issue of Nvidia and allegations that its former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, U.S. officials said. They said the talks would focus on implementing the trade agreement.
The U.S. and China in September said they would lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from the other country, without specifying an effective date. China said this month that it would only increase purchases of U.S. agricultural products if those tariffs were lowered.
However, Washington is already moving to tighten restrictions on loopholes that had given Chinese companies access to American artificial intelligence technology. So far, China's response has been to threaten countermeasures.
"If there is room for genuine U.S.-China cooperation this week, it's on managing risk rather than sharing advantage," said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. That could include cooperation on an artificial intelligence security hotline.
"Across Asia, governments under mounting pressure to pick a side will be watching Shenzhen for signs of how much room they still have to maneuver," Bhattacharya said. "Most have little appetite for a region split into two technology camps."
On Thursday, Xi is set to meet with Trump and Putin, according to Beijing's official confirmation of the event, billed as the " China-Russia-U.S. Summit ."
It's the first-ever gathering of the three leaders, albeit with low expectations that there will be sufficient time for thorough dialogue. But the event creates the opportunity for a globally influential photo-op similar to the one that Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had on the sidelines of a China-hosted Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in September 2025.
Also closely watched will be any interaction with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Last November, her comments drew Beijing's ire after indicating Tokyo would support Taiwan if the island were seriously threatened by Beijing's military.
Takaichi is expected to join the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in her first trip to China since becoming prime minister. She had met Xi on the sidelines of the APEC event last year in South Korea.
Attendees from other APEC economies are hoping for more signs of cooperation.
Anindya Bakrie, CEO of Indonesian conglomerate Bakrie & Brothers, told CNBC that when Trump and Xi meet, the narrative is hopefully one of peace and stability.
Tech issues are likely to be in heavy focus. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is set to join Trump on the Shenzhen trip. Other American executives, such as Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, joined a two-day APEC CEO Summit that kicked off Tuesday.
The APEC host city, Shenzhen, has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and is home to Huawei and BYD. The summit organizers are also using the event to showcase local robotics startups.
A slew of tech company earnings is coming out at the same time as the APEC meeting, keeping the corporate side in the spotlight as well.
Nvidia released quarterly results Wednesday morning Beijing time, following a tumultuous two weeks of scrutiny that forced the chipmaker's founder Jensen Huang to resign. The company boosted its outlook and shares rose in extended trading.
Shenzhen-based gaming and social media giant Tencent is set to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday evening. The company has previously noted constraints from its limited computing power.
U.S.-based AI giant Anthropic is pricing its highly anticipated initial public offering this week, and expected to list on the Nasdaq Thursday Nov. 19 . Its CEO Dario Amodei has urged a slowdown in AI development and warned of the risk if China does not follow suit.
—CNBC's Penny Chen and Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Xiaomi took the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max global at an event in Paris today , and it seems like the vanilla Xiaomi 18 wants a bit of the spotlight too. A tipster on X has shared what's purportedly the first live image of the phone, which you can see below.
The white unit in the photo has a metal frame and a squircle camera island with three cameras. Unlike its Pro siblings, however, there's no secondary display on the back.
The tipster also shared the phone's expected specs, which mostly (but not entirely) line up with what leaked back in September . The Xiaomi 18 is said to have a flat 6.4-inch "1.5K" 120Hz LTPO OLED with TCL's M11 panel, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, a 200MP main camera with OIS, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 50MP telephoto with OIS, along with a battery of around 7,000 mAh with 100W wired charging. It's also tipped to come with an IP69 rating, an ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, and a USB 3.2 port.
That telephoto is a bit of a departure from the September leak, which claimed the Xiaomi 18 would get a 200MP periscope with 3x optical zoom, just like the Pro models. The battery was also tipped at 7,200 mAh back then. The phone is expected to launch in China in December, so we should know for sure soon enough.

articles.title_orig: Cyber agency warns of ‘critical’ vulnerability in Java programming language
articles.title_zh: Cyber agency warns of ‘critical’ vulnerability in Java programming language
articles.content_orig:
Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK.
The 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice . The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation.
The separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch.
Security firm Calif said in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell , and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch.
Security company watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X , but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed.
Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution.
The vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix.
Oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still showed the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC.
Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security update and move to the corresponding replacement releases.
The company's Java release notes contain the update guidance, while ops.java lists the following planned builds:
The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions:
Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly.
The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw.
Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published.
The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet.
However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.
However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.
Upwind said in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis . The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64 . ARM servers do not run it.
The code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware.
Oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm said whether the Performance Pack is affected.
Both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics , which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2 , which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said.
Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions.
The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group , which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review.
Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific update addresses the issue.
Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates.
Its Java security update plan , last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release.
Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available.
This is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia posts Q3 beat as revenue rose 103% YOY to $115.8B, board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia earnings live: Nvidia posts Q3 beat as revenue rose 103% YOY to $115.8B, board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia .
The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.
By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.
Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.
Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported .
Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.
A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.
Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war .
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses .
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.
Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
It wasn't always that way.
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.
That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters .
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock .
For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge , according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.
The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales . A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.
Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund , would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported .
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported .
Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips . His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.
In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job , the Times reported.
With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.
Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's customers and employees remain committed to the company despite last week's abrupt departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang . That's the message interim CEO Colette Kress conveyed exclusively to CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after the AI chip giant delivered a quarterly beat and strong guidance.
"[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," Kress said on " Mad Money ." "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
Kress' comments came after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue and bumped up its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate to 75% from the previous 70%. It was the first earnings report since Huang's resignation as CEO amid a widening affair scandal. Shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading as the results helped ease concerns about the chipmaker's outlook following the leadership shake-up.
Some on Wall Street have wondered whether Huang's departure would prompt certain Nvidia customers to lean harder into their in-house designed chips and/or competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices .
During the "Mad Money" interview Tuesday evening, Kress emphasized that major customers have continued expressing interest in the company's products. "I have seen already with many of these [customers] contacting me and saying, 'Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand.'"
Customer demand, however, wasn't the only issue facing Nvidia. Huang's departure has also raised questions about whether the chipmaker can retain the engineers and other employees who helped build its dominance in artificial intelligence. The co-founder was widely viewed as the driving force behind Nvidia's technology and corporate culture.
Kress dismissed concerns about a potential employee exodus, stressing to Cramer that the workforce's longstanding commitment to the company is intact, and so is support from the leadership team. "The company has been built under the perspective that the employees look at Nvidia as their life work, and many of them have been here for many decades, working with us both from a technology standpoint or a business and operations perspective," she said.
"We have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy ... the work here at Nvidia," Kress told Cramer.

articles.title_orig: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.title_zh: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.content_orig:
Chief Correspondent covering media and technology
Did AI cause the US government to shut down all air travel Friday?
Could be, says the US government.
Also, maybe not. Who knows? But don't worry.
That's the confusing answer from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He went on Fox News on Monday and said that the nationwide grounding last week — as well as other recent high-profile outages at places like JPMorgan, Microsoft , and United — might have all stemmed from organizations introducing new AI software into their IT stacks.
Why does he think that? Because "one guy that's very smart with tech," — not Elon Musk, Mullin specified — told him that. And "that kinda makes sense to me."
I mean, it also kinda makes sense to me? Maybe? But I'm not running a federal agency with more than 200,000 workers and an annual budget of more than $100 billion.
But Mullin said he really doesn't know. He does know that "we just have a lot of technologists [sic] thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems. And the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."
Then Mullin told Fox viewers that they should "breathe." And be assured that the US is probably not under a cyber attack — something he felt "98%" confident about.
I would very much like to live in a world where a top federal official doesn't muddle through national news interviews about outages. I would very much like to live in a world where the administration hadn't spent much of last year telling us the federal government was incompetent and should be radically downsized . Because sometimes we really want the federal government — not "one guy" — to be able to tell us what's actually happening inside these complicated systems, and what should be done about it.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
But I also think we'd have these exact same problems if we had the most competent, well-meaning public servants in charge right now.
That's because all of this stuff is gnarly and complicated. Long before the AI boom, we've had technologists pointing out how rickety and poorly maintained much of America's digital and physical infrastructure is — and how seemingly isolated problems can have enormous ripple effects. Perhaps you recall the giant blackout of 2003 , where big swaths of the country, including New York City, lost power because of a software glitch in Ohio.
Now we've added AI to the mix —a technology so new and head-scratching that the people who are building it frequently say they're not really sure how it works , and aren't exactly sure how to control it .
Which is why people who have talked to more than "one guy" often tell us to buckle up for more instability. "We should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time," as journalist Josh Tyrangiel put it in The Atlantic .
What can you, a normal person, do about this? Here I agree with Markwayne Mullin: You shouldn't do anything. There's nothing much you can do, aside from the digital equivalent of making sure you have some soup cans and water bottles handy, just in case.
But if you're a member of the media — that is, anyone with access to a keyboard and an internet connection — things get a little trickier. It is reasonable to cover all of these outages, ask why they're happening, and not accept the hand-wavy answers you often get right after an event. But also be ready to accept that sometimes things break because things break, and that sometimes a coincidence is a coincidence. Or that maybe it's all a squirrel's fault .
That's not an easy balance to pull off. Ring the bell every time there's a possible threat, and you'll end up with a country that's permanently on edge — or worse, doesn't pay attention to any warnings at all. Wait too long before ringing the bell, and people may be woefully unprepared. It's a real challenge .
That said, one very easy step is to just stay mute when you don't have anything helpful to say.
Tuesday morning, I got asked to come on an interview show to discuss "the November 17 blackout," which confused me since I was unaware there had been a blackout Tuesday.
Turns out it was a reference to a made-up thing on social media , and I'm not going to spend more time discussing a non-thing here.
Except to say that it's one thing for your uncle to pass along a hoax email to his friends and family. And it's another to go on TV or the internet and give the hoax that much more oxygen. Even if you're ostensibly going to debunk the hoax, you're still spreading the particulates around.
But Markwayne Mullin? I'd definitely like you to ask a few more people — perhaps there are still technology experts in your organization, for starters — for more information. Then come back and tell us what you've learned. We'd love to know more.

articles.title_orig: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
articles.title_zh: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
articles.content_orig:
The prime minister earlier said he wanted to open a national debate on Britain’s relationship with the bloc
Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, spent more than two hours in the Commons taking questions on the report and Labour MPs were almost without exception positive or neutral; there was no evidence that Andy Burnham faces a significant backbench revolt any time soon. But some leftwingers are alarmed about the proposed cuts, which also concern disability groups. Frances Ryan has set out the case against in her Guardian column. Here is an extract.
double quotation mark This is in effect the creation of a two-tier welfare state, where the help you receive isn’t determined by your health but the date on your birth certificate. The £3.6bn in cuts would sever the link between need and entitlement that sits at the heart of the safety net – potentially leading to the perverse situation where two people with the same disability get unequal support simply because they’re a different age. After months of stories inflaming the narrative that feckless youngsters are feigning disability for cash, as a fashion statement or because of “social contagion”, Milburn will have felt under immense pressure to curb the youth benefits bill as a trade-off for his other large-scale spending plans. That pensioners receive roughly 55% of the welfare budget and young people (excluding children) just 2.5% is conveniently ignored.
And here is Frances’s column in full.
Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.
Andy Burnham has delayed his announcement about the possible future options for Britain forming a closer relationship with the EU until next month. (See 5.07pm .)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Liberal Democrats have today been paying tribute to John Pardoe, the former Liberal deputy leader, who has died. Ed Davey described him as “one of that small band of MPs who kept the Liberal flame burning brightly in the 1960s and 70s”. Paul Walter has more in a post at Liberal Democrat Voice.
Here is some reaction to the Milburn report from disability and health charities.
From Ross Barrett, senior policy manager at the MS Society
double quotation mark Proposals to create a new youth welfare system in place of personal independence payment (Pip) and the universal credit (UC) health element would likely mean some young people with MS losing financial support. This could be dangerous and ultimately counter-productive. Without Pip, young people will struggle to manage the overwhelming extra costs of the condition, face worsening health, and may find it harder to stay in work.
From a National Autistic Society spokesperson
double quotation mark We welcome the report’s calls for significant investment in earlier employment support and that there should be no changes to financial entitlements until that support is place. We also welcome the focus on driving down the disability employment gap, something we have been demanding for years.
For Alan Milburn’s proposed system to be effective for autistic people, it will require a very high level of autism training and understanding for anyone supporting autistic young people or deciding what they are entitled to.
From Dr Sarah Hughes, CEO of Mind,
double quotation mark Employment support on its own isn’t enough - it needs to go hand in hand with an overhaul of mental health support. It’s hugely promising to see such a clear ambition to better tailor mental health support through an open access approach that Mind has been calling for. This means that young people will be able to get support they need, on the day they need it, enabling them to get into work.
“But building a bridge to employment won’t work without an adequate benefits safety net. We’re concerned that young people with mental health problems could be left scrambling desperately to make ends meet, so we must see clear evidence that benefits will meet their essential costs. Without this, these changes could worsen mental health, make it harder to engage with support and push our young people further into the cold.
From Simon Antrobus, CEO at the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB)
double quotation mark Young people with visual impairment are twice as likely to be NEET than their peers. There is clear ambition to raise the bar of opportunity for disabled young people to pursue the careers they want. But we will only achieve the seismic change we all want to see if support is shaped by specialists who understand the unique needs and societal barriers faced by disabled young people, including those with vision impairment.
Andy Burnham has delayed his announcement about the possible options for Britain forming a closer relationship with the EU after the next election.
At Labour conference in September, Burnham said that he wanted to open a national debate on this topic, indicating that joining the customs union or the single market, or even rejoining in full, were all potential options that could be put to the public in Labour’s next manifesto.
In recent weeks, No 10 has been saying that Burnham would do this around the time of the UK-EU summit taking place that is taking place on Friday – implying soon afterwards. Whether his intervention would take the form of a speech, or a statement to MPs, or the publication of a document has not been specified.
But, in his interview with Sky’s Beth Rigby, Burnham said he was now planning to set this all out alongside his 10-year plan, “next month”. He has said the 10-year plan will be published before the Commons rises for the Christmas recess on Thursday 17 December.
double quotation mark I’m in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal. That’s what I’m doing this week [at the summit]. We’ll see how it goes.
And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. And I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.
Burnham also insisted there was no rush.
double quotation mark All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available, so that people can see the pros and cons, but [I] will set those out, in due course. There’s no rush to do that.
When it was put to him that Boris Johnson said it would be madness to reopen the debate about the UK being a member of the EU, Burnham replied:
double quotation mark I’m afraid I’m not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burnt bridges and created a lot of bad feeling. And consequently Britain has suffered as a result of that.
Andy Burnham has recorded an interview with Beth Rigby from Sky News to mark the publication of the Alan Milburn review. Here are the top lines on this topic.
Burnham described the publication of the Milburn report as a “watershed moment” for Britain. He said:
double quotation mark Let’s first be clear what this is. It’s a watershed moment. I said to the cabinet this morning, I don’t think a British cabinet has sat around that table in 50 years or more and talked about a vision for young people, support from the very early years all the way through school and then into opportunity beyond school. And that’s what this is about.
He did not rule out implementing the Milburn recommendation to cut employer national insurance for young people. (See 3.38pm. ) Asked if he would accept this idea, he replied:
double quotation mark We’re going to look at the whole of the report in the round. Some of the implications of those proposals are
